opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of headroom there, but it's not simply a matter of throwing more compute at it and hoping things get better linearly. With ShinkaEvolve, a big part of what we focused on was sample efficiency: getting strong results, like on circle packing, with a few hundred evaluations rather than thousands. Techniques like novelty-based rejection sampling, smarter parent selection that balances exploration and exploitation, and bandit-based selection over which LLM to use for a mutation all aim to make each sample count.

When you scale out massively, those ideas become even more important. Naively parallelizing gives you a lot of redundant work. Many workers rediscover the same solutions, or the archive collapses onto one mode. So the interesting questions at scale are about diversity maintenance. How do you structure islands of populations? How often do you migrate programs between them? How do you keep the archive from getting swamped by near-duplicates? It looks a lot like classic evolutionary computation, where population structure mattered enormously, except now the mutation operator is a language model that can do semantically meaningful edits.

I'm also excited about the open-endedness angle. If you have a huge compute budget, you don't have to confine yourself to one fixed objective. You can let the system build up a growing library of stepping stones, where solutions to one problem become useful ingredients for another. That's where massive scale could produce things that are qualitatively different, not just slightly better numbers on a benchmark.

The bottleneck then moves to evaluation. For problems like circle packing or competitive programming, you have cheap, reliable verifiers. For scientific discovery more broadly, like training a model or running an experiment, evaluation is expensive and noisy. So scaling the search goes hand in hand with scaling evaluation: cheaper proxies, multi-fidelity evaluation, and maybe learned evaluators. And there's the risk of reward hacking. The more search pressure you apply, the more likely the system is to find loopholes in your objective. Robust evaluation design becomes a central research problem, not an afterthought.

So I'm optimistic. I think we've only scratched the surface. But the gains from scale will come from pairing it with better search structure, better diversity mechanisms, and better evaluators, and that's part of why we open-sourced it. We want the community to push on exactly these questions.

r001.rationale: The response says massive compute could enable open-ended search beyond a fixed objective, building a growing library of stepping stones that become useful for other problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot at Sakana. The way I'd frame it is that ShinkaEvolve, at its core, is an evolutionary search where the mutation operator is an LLM. You have a population of programs, you sample parents, you ask the model to propose a change, you evaluate it, and you keep what works. And the interesting thing about that setup is that it's embarrassingly parallel in a way that gradient descent is not. Every evaluation is independent. Every mutation proposal is independent. So in principle, if you give me ten thousand GPUs or ten thousand API workers, I can run ten thousand evaluations in parallel and the whole thing just scales out.

But I'd actually push back a little on the idea that raw scale is the thing that matters most. When we built Shinka, a big part of the motivation was sample efficiency. Earlier systems in this space were using tens of thousands of evaluations to find a good solution, and we were getting comparable or better results in a few hundred. So the question for me isn't just "what happens if you throw a hundred times more compute at it," it's "what happens if you throw a hundred times more compute at something that's already sample efficient." And I think the answer is that you unlock qualitatively different problems, not just the same problems faster.

Concretely, there are a few axes where scale helps. One is population diversity. If you have a small population, you tend to collapse onto one or two lineages and you get stuck in a local optimum. With a massive population and good novelty filtering, you can maintain many parallel threads of exploration, almost like islands in the classical island model, and occasionally cross-pollinate between them. Second is the expense of the evaluation itself. Right now most of our tasks have evaluations that run in seconds or minutes. But the really interesting problems, things like training a small model end to end as the fitness function, or running a long scientific simulation, those are hours. Those only become feasible when you can afford to run thousands of them concurrently. And third, scaling lets you use a portfolio of LLMs more aggressively. One thing we do in Shinka is adaptive model selection, bandit-style, where the system learns which model is giving useful mutations for a given problem. With more parallelism you can explore that space much more thoroughly.

The honest caveat is that scaling exposes bottlenecks you don't see at small scale. The archive and the parent selection become a central point of contention. If everything is reporting back to a single database, that's your bottleneck. You end up wanting something more asynchronous and decentralized, which actually looks a lot like the old distributed evolutionary computation literature from the nineties, just with a very different mutation operator. The other issue is that the evaluation can become the bottleneck in a different sense: if your fitness function is noisy, scaling just gives you more noise unless you handle it statistically.

And then the thing I'm personally most excited about is closing the loop. If you're generating millions of program variants with scores attached, that's a training signal. You can fine-tune the proposing model on what actually worked, and then the next round of search is better. That's where I think massive scale stops being "search" and starts to look like something closer to open-ended discovery, where the system is improving its own capacity to improve. We're not fully there yet, but I think the ingredients are on the table.

r001.rationale: The candidate says massive scale could move the system from search toward “open-ended discovery,” where it improves its own capacity to improve.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential, but the interesting question is whether you’re just generating more candidates or actually exploring a broader space of ideas. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing. If every search starts from the same solution and gets very similar feedback, you could spend a lot more compute rediscovering the same improvements.

What I’d be excited about is running populations that explore different directions, with some mechanism for sharing useful discoveries between them. You want enough communication that a good idea can spread, but enough independence that everything doesn’t collapse onto one approach too early.

And then evaluation becomes really important. Can you evaluate candidates cheaply enough to sustain that scale? And does your evaluator capture what you actually care about? Otherwise, you’re scaling the ability to exploit a benchmark rather than solve the underlying problem.

So I’d want to understand the scaling curve empirically: as we increase the budget, how much additional improvement do we get, and how does that depend on how we organize the search? That’s where I think it gets really interesting—whether more compute buys us qualitatively different solutions, rather than just more attempts.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scaling could explore a broader space of ideas and yield qualitatively different solutions, describing diverse searches that share discoveries while remaining independent. This communicates movement toward genuinely open-ended search.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential, but the interesting question is what you scale. You can run more candidate evaluations in parallel, but you can also run independent populations that explore different approaches and occasionally exchange discoveries. That gives you a way to preserve diversity instead of spending the entire budget refining one promising idea.

The challenge is that more compute doesn’t automatically translate into better search. You need a reliable evaluation signal, and you need to allocate resources between exploring new ideas and improving the ones that already work. Otherwise, you can end up generating lots of variations that don’t teach you very much—or getting better at exploiting weaknesses in your evaluator.

So I’d be excited to study the scaling behavior systematically: as we increase the budget, where do improvements come from? More attempts, longer evolutionary trajectories, or better coordination between searches? If we can understand that, we can make scaling much more deliberate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling parallel evaluations and diverse populations to explore approaches, but it does not say that scaling could move Shinka Evolve toward genuinely open-ended search.
